nodes.en: Parametric Human Bodies: SMPL and SMPL-X
nodes.title: 参数化人体：姿态、体型与全局轨迹
nodes.summary: 参数化人体：姿态、体型与全局轨迹
nodes.definition: A parametric human body model represents a body mesh using a compact set of pose and shape parameters. Pose describes articulated joint rotations; shape describes body proportions. A global translation and orientation place the person in a chosen world frame. This representation makes motion estimated from video or motion capture comparable across frames and subjects. Its skeleton and joint conventions are human conventions, so its parameters are not robot joint commands. Converting the sequence into a robot reference requires an explicit embodiment mapping and coordinate conversion.
nodes.example: An estimated sequence may contain a global pelvis trajectory, rotations for human joints, and a fixed body-shape vector. To imitate it on a G1, first identify the coordinate frame and human joint convention; then solve for robot configurations matching selected body targets.
nodes.role_en: Common interface between monocular human-motion recovery, motion datasets, and retargeting; the human representation can also be bypassed by newer direct video-to-robot methods.

notation.meaning: Human mesh vertices in the model frame.

nodes.title: 人体到机器人动作重定向
nodes.summary: 人体到机器人动作重定向
nodes.definition: Motion retargeting computes robot configurations that reproduce selected properties of a source motion despite different limb lengths, joint axes, joint limits, and degrees of freedom. A typical formulation matches body positions or orientations subject to robot constraints. The source and target need consistent reference frames, scale, and anatomical correspondences. Retargeting is usually a kinematic computation: a pose can satisfy its objective while still violating balance or contact dynamics. Physical execution therefore needs motion refinement, a controller, and validation of contact and actuation feasibility.
nodes.example: A human foot target can be reachable for the human but outside the robot leg workspace. A constrained inverse-kinematics solve trades off pelvis, foot, and hand errors while respecting joint limits. Inspect the resulting sequence before using it as an RL tracking reference.
nodes.role_en: Connects human-motion recovery and datasets to robot imitation. It is the explicit conversion stage studied by GMR and an alternative to direct video-to-robot prediction.

notation.meaning: Robot generalized configuration.

nodes.title: 全身参考动作跟踪
nodes.summary: 全身参考动作跟踪
nodes.definition: A motion-tracking controller uses the current robot state and a reference trajectory to generate actions that follow the desired body motion. Tracking can include joint angles, body positions, orientations, velocities, and contact events. Reinforcement learning commonly combines tracking rewards with regularization and physical constraints in a simulator. The reference describes desired motion, while the policy determines actions under disturbances and actuation limits. Good tracking of a reference does not establish successful object interaction; ball contact and post-contact recovery need additional task measurements.
nodes.example: For a kicking reference, a controller may track pelvis orientation and foot pose until the strike. A complete trial also checks whether the actual foot reaches the ball, whether the robot remains upright after impact, and whether the ball reaches its commanded destination.
nodes.role_en: Provides the executable low-level controller used by BeyondMimic, motion-guided soccer, teleoperation, and human-video imitation.

notation.meaning: Measured or simulated robot feature k.

nodes.en: Motion Priors: Tracking, Adversarial and Latent
nodes.title: 动作先验：跟踪、对抗与潜空间
nodes.summary: 动作先验：跟踪、对抗与潜空间
nodes.definition: A motion prior restricts or rewards behavior according to demonstrations of plausible movement. Tracking priors reward agreement with a particular time-indexed reference. Adversarial priors learn to distinguish motion transitions from demonstrations and policy rollouts, then supply an imitation reward. Latent priors encode a reusable space of motions that a task policy can command. These approaches differ in how demonstrations constrain timing and behavior. A motion prior encourages properties present in its data; it does not by itself guarantee dynamic stability, object contact, or task success.
nodes.example: A soccer controller can receive a task reward for moving the ball toward a goal and a motion-prior reward for human-like body transitions. Increasing the prior weight changes the tradeoff. Measure ball outcomes and falls rather than treating a natural-looking movement as sufficient evidence.
nodes.role_en: Explains how DeepMimic, AMP, HumanX, humanoid goalkeeping, and soccerbot use human movement differently; these are parallel design choices rather than one mandatory sequence.

nodes.title: 动作质量与物理可执行性
nodes.summary: 动作质量与物理可执行性
nodes.definition: Motion quality must be checked in several independent dimensions: source fidelity, geometric validity, temporal continuity, contact consistency, and performance under physical execution. A low inverse-kinematics error does not imply feasible torques or stable balance. Foot skating occurs when a supposed stance foot moves relative to the ground; penetration and abrupt joint changes can also enter a retargeted reference. Quantitative checks should accompany complete rendered sequences and closed-loop tests. Report kinematic validation, simulator success, and real-robot execution as separate evidence levels.
nodes.example: For a ten-second motion, plot joint velocity and stance-foot speed, inspect a fixed-camera replay, and then run the controller for the complete duration. A clip that survives a tracking rollout may still have poor source fidelity or unacceptable post-contact sway.
nodes.role_en: Connects GMR reference quality, motion tracking robustness, simulator contacts, and the distinction between reference generation and successful robot deployment.

notation.meaning: Indicator that foot k is expected to be in stationary ground contact.

nodes.title: 球状态估计与可见性
nodes.summary: 球状态估计与可见性
nodes.definition: A soccer controller needs the ball position and often its velocity in a specified frame, even when vision is delayed, noisy, or temporarily unavailable. Camera detections provide image coordinates rather than direct metric state; depth, geometry, or other sensors supply additional constraints. An estimator combines dynamics predictions with timestamped measurements and should expose uncertainty. The sensor setup matters: external motion capture, RGB, depth, infrared reflectance, and LiDAR provide different information. A successful controller under one setup is not evidence of the same autonomy under another.
nodes.example: A ball disappears behind the robot foot for several frames. The estimator propagates its current velocity hypothesis, then corrects the estimate when a new observation arrives. A missed observation and a measured stationary ball must remain different cases in the controller input.
nodes.role_en: Foundation for reactive kicking, interception, active vision, and simulator perception models. Each paper should state which sensors are available at deployment.

notation.meaning: Ball position and velocity in the declared frame.

nodes.title: 脚球碰撞、踢球与运球动力学
nodes.summary: 脚球碰撞、踢球与运球动力学
nodes.definition: Kicking transfers momentum through a short contact event, while dribbling repeatedly regulates ball motion through intermittent contacts. The outcome depends on relative foot velocity, contact point, foot orientation, ball properties, surface friction, and the robot support state. These interactions can be modeled by impulse and contact constraints or learned through simulation experience. High ball speed alone does not establish a useful kick: direction accuracy, recovery, and repeated execution matter. Simulator parameters and contact timing strongly affect the transfer of these skills to hardware.
nodes.example: A faster swing may increase ball speed while reducing target accuracy or destabilizing the stance leg. Compare complete trials using the same target distance and initial ball distribution, and record shot placement, contact misses, robot falls, and the state after recovery.
nodes.role_en: Physical basis for RoboNaldo, PAiD, dribbling, passing, and goalkeeper contact. Links task rewards to contact simulation and robot dynamics.

notation.meaning: Ball mass.

nodes.title: 腿式交互中的主动视觉
nodes.summary: 腿式交互中的主动视觉
nodes.definition: Active vision makes sensing direction part of the control problem. A robot can turn its head, neck, torso, or body to retain useful observations while it approaches or interacts with the ball. Visibility depends on camera field of view, occlusion, body pose, and the scene. Training can model those effects or optimize sensor motion jointly with locomotion. This differs from simply attaching a camera to a policy: actions influence what can be observed next, so sensing and movement are coupled through time.
nodes.example: During a sharp dribbling turn, pointing the camera only along the body heading may lose the ball. A policy can coordinate neck rotation and foot placement so that the ball stays observable while changing direction. Hardware actuator range and camera latency still constrain this behavior.
nodes.role_en: Common comparison axis for Dribble Master, Joga, and DAVIS. Their sensor models and real hardware differ, so visibility-aware policies are related rather than identical.

nodes.title: 技能接口与切换状态分布
nodes.summary: 技能接口与切换状态分布
nodes.definition: A skill interface specifies the commands accepted by a low-level policy and the states in which that policy can start and stop reliably. Chaining dribbling, passing, shooting, and recovery requires compatibility between the terminal state distribution of one skill and the initial-state distribution of the next. A valid command format does not guarantee such compatibility. Policies can be trained on states visited by preceding skills, or share a common locomotion substrate. Timing and observation history also matter because the robot may switch while moving.
nodes.example: A shooting policy trained only from stationary starts may fail when invoked mid-stride during dribbling. Collect handoff states from the dribbling controller, train or fine-tune the shot from those states, and evaluate the complete dribble-to-shot sequence.
nodes.role_en: Connects hierarchical soccer planning to executable controllers. Joga uses distributional skill chaining; locomotion-grounded soccer uses a shared locomotion hub; RoboNaldo exposes locomotion and kick-trigger commands.

nodes.title: 多智能体足球与团队协作
nodes.summary: 多智能体足球与团队协作
nodes.definition: Multi-agent soccer introduces other learning or scripted players into a physical control problem. Each agent acts from its own observations, while game outcomes depend on interactions among teammates, opponents, and the ball. Self-play provides changing opponents; population training can reduce overfitting to a single strategy. Team coordination requires more than stable locomotion or accurate kicking, because positioning, passing, and defending operate over longer horizons. Evaluation should separate individual motor skills, one-versus-one play, and cooperative team performance under specified observation and communication assumptions.
nodes.example: Two robots with identical kicking controllers can behave differently when one pursues the ball continuously and the other preserves defensive positioning. Evaluate game outcomes across multiple opponents and seeds, while checking whether perception and communication are local or externally supplied.
nodes.role_en: Links low-level control to the simulated football hierarchy and OP3 one-versus-one self-play. Provides a separate branch for tactics rather than treating tactics as a byproduct of every soccer skill paper.

nodes.title: DeepMimic：示例引导的物理动作控制
nodes.summary: DeepMimic：示例引导的物理动作控制
nodes.definition: DeepMimic trains simulated articulated characters to imitate reference motion while pursuing task goals. The policy observes the character state and reference phase, and reinforcement learning rewards agreement with the example as well as task performance. The method connects motion-capture specification to physical feedback control: disturbances change the actual rollout, and the policy supplies corrective actions. It demonstrates diverse characters and dynamic skills, including recovery. These experiments establish a simulation-based imitation method; a rendered Atlas-like character is not evidence of deployment on a physical humanoid robot.
nodes.example: For a simulated kick, a motion clip specifies the desired style and a task reward specifies the target. Perturb the character during execution and compare its feedback response with direct playback of reference joint angles. Only the former can adapt actions to the altered state.
nodes.role_en: Historical foundation for reference tracking, recovery, and motion-guided robot-soccer curricula. It is a predecessor conceptually, not an assertion that every later system reuses its exact implementation.

nodes.title: AMP：对抗动作先验
nodes.summary: AMP：对抗动作先验
nodes.definition: AMP learns a motion-style reward from demonstration transitions rather than requiring the controller to follow one predetermined clip and phase. A discriminator separates demonstration transitions from policy-generated transitions, and its output supplies an imitation signal during reinforcement learning. A task reward still specifies what the character should accomplish. This enables unstructured motion datasets to guide style without explicit clip selection. The original work evaluates physics-based simulated characters; later humanoid soccer methods adapt the adversarial-prior idea to robot embodiments and interaction tasks.
nodes.example: A dataset contains running and turning transitions. A soccer policy receives a ball-progress task reward and an adversarial style reward. It can choose movement transitions according to the task rather than advancing through one fixed running clip.
nodes.role_en: Explains the adversarial human-motion prior used in reactive soccer, DAVIS, and humanoid goalkeeping; it is distinct from time-indexed motion tracking.

nodes.title: PHC：持续动作跟踪与跌倒恢复
nodes.summary: PHC：持续动作跟踪与跌倒恢复
nodes.definition: PHC addresses continuous reference-driven control of simulated humanoid avatars when reference poses are noisy and unexpected falls occur. Its progressive multiplicative control policy adds capacity to learn harder motions and recovery without discarding previously acquired skills. The controller can continue following references rather than requiring a reset after every failure. This is especially relevant when motion originates from video estimation or generated motion instead of a clean capture sequence. The system concerns physical simulation of avatars; robust simulated recovery does not establish the same behavior on a real G1.
nodes.example: Feed a noisy video-estimated pose sequence into the simulated controller, disturb the avatar, and observe whether it recovers and resumes tracking. Evaluate both recovery and reference error over the uninterrupted sequence rather than terminating at the first fall.
nodes.role_en: Reusable foundation for large motion libraries, recovery policies, and noisy human-motion interfaces; PHC is also one retargeting baseline considered by GMR.

nodes.title: GVHMR：重力视角坐标下的人体动作恢复
nodes.summary: GVHMR：重力视角坐标下的人体动作恢复
nodes.definition: GVHMR recovers human motion in a world coordinate system from monocular video. It predicts poses in a gravity-view coordinate system defined by gravity and the camera viewing direction, reducing ambiguity associated with arbitrary world orientations. Camera rotations then transform the estimates into world-grounded motion. Per-frame pose estimation avoids the same autoregressive accumulation mechanism as methods that repeatedly predict relative pose updates. The output is human motion suitable for downstream processing, not an executable robot controller; camera and motion-estimation errors can propagate into retargeting.
nodes.example: A moving-camera soccer video contains both camera motion and a person’s kick. Recover a world-grounded human sequence, inspect its ground alignment and global trajectory, and then retarget it. A plausible camera-view overlay alone does not verify the world trajectory or robot balance.
nodes.role_en: Upstream video-to-human-motion component for demonstration preparation; connects camera geometry and human body models to GMR-style retargeting.

nodes.definition: Retargeting Matters systematically studies how the quality of human-to-robot reference motions affects downstream humanoid tracking. Its General Motion Retargeting method maps multiple human motion formats to diverse robot embodiments with inverse-kinematics-based processing. The evaluation holds the BeyondMimic tracking setup comparatively fixed to isolate retargeting effects instead of allowing extensive reward tuning to hide reference defects. Foot sliding, penetration, and infeasible movement can reduce robustness even when many frames appear plausible. The retargeter produces references; the tracking policy supplies physical feedback actions.
nodes.example: Retarget the same LAFAN1 sequence with different methods and train trackers under matched settings. Compare source fidelity, contacts, complete sequence success, and recovery. An accurate-looking isolated frame cannot establish that a long dynamic reference is executable.
nodes.role_en: The requested General Motion Retargeting branch; separates kinematic reference conversion from policy tracking and links directly to BeyondMimic and TWIST.

nodes.title: TWIST：全身动作模仿遥操作
nodes.summary: TWIST：全身动作模仿遥操作
nodes.definition: TWIST builds whole-body humanoid teleoperation around human motion imitation. It first retargets motion-capture sequences into robot references and then learns a unified whole-body controller with reinforcement learning and behavior cloning. Its analysis distinguishes privileged future reference information available during training from the signals usable by a responsive deployed controller. The resulting system covers locomotion, legged manipulation, whole-body manipulation, and expressive motion. Teleoperation supplies the intended movement; robust reference execution is not the same problem as autonomous task planning or language-conditioned decision making.
nodes.example: A human operator changes from walking to a whole-body reaching movement. The retargeting interface converts the human pose into a robot reference, and the controller tracks it while maintaining physical feedback. Check reference latency and whether the deployed policy uses future frames.
nodes.role_en: Concrete path from GMR and imitation learning to real humanoid control; useful for collecting robot demonstrations for later autonomy.

nodes.definition: HumanX converts short human videos into robot interaction skills through two coordinated components. XGen builds anchor-centric interaction data and augments it to expand plausible robot-object configurations. XMimic emphasizes interaction-critical parts of imitation when learning the controller. The framework targets anchorable interactions rather than assuming any arbitrary video can directly become an executable policy. The October 2026 abstract reports nine skills across basketball, football, badminton, cargo pickup, and reactive fighting with zero-shot G1 transfer. Task-specific external sensing assumptions must still be read for each demonstration.
nodes.example: For a demonstrated ball interaction, preserve the relation between the striking body part and the ball while varying admissible starting configurations. Evaluate the learned controller on new interaction states and complete exchanges. A successful open-loop shot and a perception-conditioned passing exchange are different tests.
nodes.role_en: Connects recovered human motion, contact-preserving augmentation, and humanoid soccer interaction. The current v2 reports nine skills; counts in older project material may differ.

nodes.definition: BeyondRetarget studies a direct route from monocular RGB video to robot motion. Instead of requiring an explicit estimated human body sequence followed by a separate retargeter, it learns robot-oriented implicit representations and applies contact-aware motion optimization. This design aims to reduce errors that become fixed when human-motion estimation and retargeting are separate stages. The paper reports simulation and real humanoid execution comparisons. Its generated motion still needs a controller and physical evaluation; bypassing a human representation does not eliminate monocular ambiguity or robot constraints.
nodes.example: Compare two pipelines on the same video: human recovery followed by GMR, and direct robot-motion prediction. Check contact continuity, reference accuracy, latency, and complete controller execution. A lower prediction loss does not by itself establish better balance or safer impact behavior.
nodes.role_en: Alternative branch to the GVHMR-to-GMR pipeline. It changes the representation and optimization boundary rather than replacing the need for robot physics or tracking.

nodes.summary: 分层学习：从运动控制到模拟团队足球
nodes.definition: This work integrates imitation learning, individual reinforcement learning, multi-agent reinforcement learning, and population-based training into physically simulated humanoid football. Learning proceeds across temporal scales: low-level natural movement supports intermediate ball skills, which support team behavior over longer horizons. Transferable behavioral representations connect these stages. The contribution is the integration of motor control and coordinated decisions rather than a new camera-based ball detector or physical humanoid deployment. Its avatars operate in a simulated multi-agent setting; hardware and egocentric perception claims should not be imported from later robot soccer systems.
nodes.example: Compare a policy trained only to move naturally with one trained to dribble and then play with teammates. Running quality, ball skill, and team decisions need separate measurements. A goal can depend on teammate positioning even when the individual motor controller is unchanged.

nodes.en: Learning Agile Soccer Skills for a Bipedal Robot
nodes.title: OP3：深度强化学习的一对一足球
nodes.summary: OP3：深度强化学习的一对一足球
nodes.definition: This work trains a miniature humanoid with twenty actuated joints to play a simplified one-versus-one soccer game. Reinforcement learning produces locomotion, turning, kicking, fall recovery, and basic game-dependent behavior that transfer from simulation to physical OP3 robots. Skill reuse and multi-agent learning connect robust movement to longer-horizon game objectives. The setup is important: the original real-game state information includes an external motion-capture system, so it should not be described as fully onboard vision-only soccer. Robot size, control rate, and task definition also differ from full-size G1 systems.
nodes.example: Observe a robot fall, recover, pursue the ball, and block an opponent within one game. Evaluate both recovery and scoring against matched opponents. The result does not imply that the same network can run unchanged on a G1 or perceive the ball from its own camera.
nodes.role_en: Soccer research branch: Real miniature-humanoid soccer with learned agile skills, recovery, and basic tactical behavior.
